chapters.title: The front door
chapters.summary: What slopcad is, what the home page shows you, and where the workbench lives.

cues.text: Welcome to slopcad. Before any modeling, a quick map of where everything lives.
The headline is the promise: parametric CAD whose document always tells the truth.
The right panel renders the guide plate live — your browser is the CAD engine.
This button, Open the workbench, is the door to the modeling cockpit.
Three cards below index the app: Workbench, Components, and Docs.
Components opens reusable parametric parts, rebuilt live by the kernel.
Docs holds every guide, generated from the constants the test gates prove.
The dot beside the buttons is the API light. Green means the server answers.
Come through the door. The workbench loads the boot plate document.

chapters.title: Drawing your first sketch
chapters.summary: Entering the sketch workspace through the command menu, the drawing tools, and saving a rectangle.

cues.text: The cockpit: toolbar on top, model tree left, timeline strip below.
Every command hides behind this menu button. Click it to open the palette.
The palette lists every verb the workbench ships. A row runs on click.
Find the Sketch row and click it: it opens the 2D drawing workspace.
Sketch mode: a gridded canvas replaces the 3D view. Squares are 10 mm.
The first cluster holds the drawing tools: line, circle, rectangle, point.
Click the rectangle tool to arm it. The status strip confirms the tool.
Click once to drop the first corner. The grid reads out in millimeters.
Click the opposite corner. The rectangle commits as one closed profile.
Save returns to the model. The sketch is now a record solid features use.

chapters.title: From profile to solid
chapters.summary: Turning a sketch into a 3D pad, reading the timeline, and undo/redo as the safety net.

cues.text: Start from the fresh boot plate. Every session opens on this document.
The Sketch button in the top bar is the second door into the workspace.
The 20 by 15 rectangle again: arm the tool, one click per corner.
With a closed profile in place, Extrude turns the sketch into a solid.
The pad rises at the default depth of ten millimeters, back in 3D.
The timeline is the recipe: translate, rotate, extrude. Every chip is editable.
Undo removes the pad. The document falls back to the plate, nothing lost.
Redo brings the pad straight back. History is the safety net while you explore.
That is the core loop: sketch a profile, extrude it, then edit via history.

chapters.title: The base tools
chapters.summary: Select, Measure, and Rotate in the toolbar, the digit shortcuts, and Escape to cancel.

cues.text: Three verbs live beside the document plate: Select, Measure, Rotate.
Each button wears its digit. One, two, three arm the tools in order.
The status bar echoes the live tool: tool = select (active).
Click Measure. The button stays pressed while the tool is live.
The status bar flips too: tool = measure (active).
Escape cancels a live tool. Focus the viewport, then press it.
Rotate arms the same way — click it and the pressed state moves.
Now the shortcut: with the toolbar focused, press the digit.
Any tool, any time: click it, press its digit, or Escape away.

chapters.title: Selecting and inspecting
chapters.summary: Picking a body, reading the Properties and Measurement panels, and editing a parameter.

cues.text: The right rail: Properties, Parameters, then the Measurement block.
With nothing selected, the Properties panel says so — honestly.
In the model tree, click the plate body. It lights up selected.
Properties answers: name, id, kind — and the feature that produces it.
Measurement reads the solid live: bounds, volume, area.
Parameters holds the driving numbers. Find holeDiameter — 8 today.
Click the field, select all, type 10, then Apply.
The bore widens on screen and the volume drops. Geometry follows.
The timeline summary still reads 2 valid — the edit re-ran cleanly.

chapters.title: Undo, redo, and rollback
chapters.summary: The history buttons, the timeline's rollback points, and clearing a selection.

cues.text: One quick pad gives the history something to walk. Sketch, draw, extrude.
The History group holds Undo and Redo — the document's cursor.
Undo: the pad leaves, the timeline falls back a chip.
Redo brings it straight back — no rework, no loss.
Between the timeline chips sit gaps — each a rollback point.
Click the gap after translate. The marker drops in.
Everything after the marker parks — dashed, out of the recipe.
The command menu's History group: Remove rollback point.
The chain re-executes — 3 valid — and the pad is back.
One more history verb: pick the plate body in the tree.
Clear selection — the menu's deselect — empties the panels again.

chapters.title: Deleting features
chapters.summary: Upstream features refuse deletion; leaves delete; undo restores them exactly.

cues.text: The boot plate is a recipe: translate, then rotate, both feeding the plate.
Select the translate feature — the upstream step — in the tree.
Properties shows a Delete feature action for the selected feature.
Click it — and the domain refuses: rotate references this feature.
The refusal is verbatim, and nothing was issued — the log stands.
Now the leaf: select the rotate feature.
Delete feature commits. The timeline falls to translate alone.
The document recomputes: the plate now depends on translate alone.
Undo restores the leaf exactly — deletes are history too.

chapters.title: Display modes and the zoom window
chapters.summary: Shaded, +Edges, Wire, and Hidden — plus dragging a zoom window.

cues.text: The view panel sits bottom-right: navigation above, display below.
Shaded is the boot mode — solid faces, lit, no edges.
Click +Edges: the model's edges overlay the faces.
Wire strips to edges alone — pure topology.
Hidden-line gives the technical-drawing look.
Back to Shaded for the rest of the tour.
Set a standard view first — Front — then arm the zoom window.
The magnifier arms the zoom window — the viewport says how.
Drag a box over the plate. Release to commit.
The camera halves its distance — the model fills the window.

chapters.title: The camera: orbit, views, fit
chapters.summary: Orbiting by drag, the standard views, first and third-angle, fit, and look-at.

cues.text: The camera opens on the document's spec view. Drag the canvas to orbit.
You own the camera now — the tiny cube tracks your corner.
The reset arrow returns the camera to the document spec.
Front is exact: azimuth 270, elevation 0.
Top looks straight down the z axis.
Iso frames the near corner — the modeling default.
The frame icon flips the drafting convention. Click it once.
First-angle moves the iso corner by ninety degrees.
Back to third-angle — the views keep their letters.
Fit frames the model's bounds exactly.
Look-at needs a selection — the crosshair is dim until one exists.
Pick the plate in the tree, click the crosshair — the camera centers.

chapters.title: Section clipping
chapters.summary: Cutting the model at a plane and reading the true face it leaves.

cues.text: The Measurement block ends in two small buttons: section, view cut.
Section rides a selected body. Pick the plate in the tree.
Click section. The clip plane sits at the plate's mid-height.
The Section row measures the true cut face: about 550 mm².
The centroid line gives the face's center: x 15, y 10, z 5.
View cut removes the kept half — cap faces close the solid.
The volume readout halves: you are looking inside the plate.
Toggle section off — the rows leave with the plane.
A section is a view state: measured, honest, and reversible.

chapters.title: Appearances and lighting
chapters.summary: Body appearances from the tree palette, the light rigs, and quality mode.

cues.text: The palette dot on the plate's tree row opens appearances.
The library: steel, brass, copper, anodized blue, carbon, ceramic.
Click Brass.
The plate renders brass — and the chip carries its color.
None returns the scene default.
Lower in the view panel: three light rigs — Studio, North, Inspect.
Inspect is one hard light — flattening, but honest.
Studio wraps the model in soft, even light.
Render quality: Standard is the deterministic default.
Quality opts into soft shadows and ambient occlusion.
Back to Standard — fast and reproducible.

chapters.title: Sketching on a face
chapters.summary: Selecting a solid face, sketching on it, and editing the driving feature by number.

cues.text: Fresh plate. Sketch a rectangle and extrude the base pad.
To build on a face, first select it: click the pad's top face.
The selection reads face|body_extrude — a real face, addressed.
The command menu's Sketch on face keys on that face selection.
The sketch editor boots ON the face — its datum resolves true.
Draw a rectangle on the face, then extrude: a pad on the pad.
The pad doubles — the readout adds it to plate and base.
Driving-face edit: raise extrudeDepth to 15 and Apply.
The datum lifts with the number — and the face's pad follows.
Faces are anchor surfaces: select one, sketch on it, edit by number.

chapters.title: Sweep: profile along a path
chapters.summary: Saving a profile and a path sketch, sweeping them into a tube, and undo/redo on features.

cues.text: The OpenCascade workbench: same tools, a kernel that sweeps.
Sketch one: a 20 × 20 square. Save it — sweeps need a profile.
The path must START at the sketch origin — the tool pins it there.
Then run it straight up 40 millimeters — the sweep's spine.
Two sketches saved, the Sweep row unlocks. Profile and path: its inputs.
Point the form at sketch 1 for the profile, sketch 2 for the path.
Create. The kernel sweeps the square along the spine.
The tube lands on its analytic pin, beside the boot plate.
The timeline chip says sweep — a real feature, not a mesh.
Undo removes the sweep; the timeline falls back a chip.
Redo brings the tube straight back — history holds features.
Profile plus path: the sweep recipe. Next, lofts join two profiles.

chapters.title: Loft: skinning two sections
chapters.summary: Two section sketches, one skinned solid on Simpson's rule, and a station edit that re-drives it.

cues.text: A fresh OCCT document for the loft: two sections, one solid.
Section one: a 20 × 20 square — the loft's wide end.
Section two: a 10 × 10 square, saved as the narrow end.
The Loft form pre-seeds its two oldest sketches — exactly ours.
Create, and the kernel skins a taper between the sections.
Simpson's rule pins the taper — it lands beside the plate.
Every section is a station: loftZ_1 lifts the top to 50.
Apply re-drives — the taper stretches to its 50 mm pin.
Loft: two sketches, one skinned transition, live stations.

chapters.title: Helix: a swept coil
chapters.summary: The meridian cross-section, the sketch-pool gate, and the helical sweep on its derived band.

cues.text: The OCCT workbench again — this time a helical sweep.
Draw a tiny rectangle beside the axis: the thread's cross-section.
Save it. Feature rows gate on a pool of two sketches or more.
A one-line throwaway sketch unlocks the gate.
Open Helix and point it at the meridian explicitly: sketch 1.
Create. The meridian sweeps helically around the axis.
The coil lands inside its derived band — turns, radius, meridian.
One cross-section plus turns: screw geometry. Threads come next.

chapters.title: Threads and their history
chapters.summary: The thread feature on its containment band, a deeper re-drive, and walking it in history.

cues.text: The ⌀6 rod at the origin — the thread cuts on the world Z axis.
The Thread form targets the extrusion by default. Create.
The ISO profile cuts a groove — inside the derived band.
threadLength1 goes to 8; Apply re-drives the cut deeper.
Deeper thread, less material — the volume drops on schedule.
The last transaction was the edit: undo reverts just the number.
A second undo removes the thread feature itself.
Redo restores it — valid, and back in the timeline.
Threads are features: cut, re-drive, and walk them in history.

chapters.title: Draft, rib, and scale
chapters.summary: Tapering an extrusion, unioning a rib stiffener, and scaling cubically — each re-driven.

cues.text: Three shaping features, one family. Draft first: a saved ⌀6 circle.
The throwaway line sketch unlocks the feature rows.
Draft extrudes the circle with a 5-degree taper — Create.
A frustum, not a cylinder — the taper lands beside the plate.
extrudeTaper1 to 0 and Apply: the taper flattens to the rod.
Rib next, on a fresh rod. Sketch its section: a low 10 × 1 bar.
Save, add the throwaway, open Rib, pick the section: sketch 1.
The rib unions onto the rod — material added, one feature.
ribThickness to 4 re-drives: more rib, more volume.
Scale last: another fresh rod, the Scale form, Create.
Factor 2 doubles each axis — the rod's volume times eight.
Factor 3: the rod times 27. Apply and watch it land.
Draft shapes walls, ribs stiffen, scale sizes — all parametric.

chapters.title: Thicken and split
chapters.summary: Hollowing a rod into its exact shell, and splitting a body by a datum plane.

cues.text: Hollow and cut. First the ⌀6 rod, then the Thicken form.
Wall thickness 1 mm — Create.
The rod becomes its own 1 mm shell, beside the plate.
Split next: a fresh rod and a datum plane at z = 5.
Origin z = 5, Create datum — a cutting plane through the mid.
The Split form cuts by the plane. Create keeps one side.
Exactly half the rod stays — cut true, beside the plate.
splitSide -1 flips the kept half — same volume, other side.
Thicken hollows, split divides — both re-drivable by number.

chapters.title: Holes and patterns
chapters.summary: The structured hole form and its ghost, positions sketches, linear patterns, and mirrors.

cues.text: Holes and repeats. First a 30 × 20 plate, extruded ten.
The Hole form is structured: type, size, position — no sketch.
Pick Counterbore, set the position to 55, 25.
A ghost previews the cut; Create lands the analytic pin.
Fresh plate, and a sketch of two points — holes by position.
Point the form at the sketch: two glyphs, one feature.
Create cuts both holes — one feature, many positions.
Patterns: a fresh rod, the Pattern form, skip one instance.
Three placed, one skipped: two rods, beside the plate.
Count 5, spacing 30 — the array re-drives to four rods.
Mirror last: a fresh rod, a datum plane at x = 35.
The Mirror form with merge on: the reflection unions in.
mirrorMerge to 1: Apply leaves the reflection standing alone.
Structure the hole, sketch the positions, pattern the bodies.

chapters.title: Booleans and moving bodies
chapters.summary: Subtract, union, and the volume-invariant body move — through the command surface.

cues.text: Boolean ops. A 60 × 40 plate, then a ⌀10 cylinder inside it.
The Boolean form subtracts by default. Check pad 2, Create.
The cylinder is gone — the holed plate, beside the plate.
Union: two 30 × 40 plates that share an edge.
Switch the op to Union (join), check pad 2, Create.
One slab — 60 by 40 by 10, beside the boot plate.
Move body: translation, not geometry. The rod again.
Offset x = 10, Create.
The body slides — the volume holds. Moves are transforms.
Subtract removes, union joins, move transports — all features.

chapters.title: The surface pipeline
chapters.summary: Base sheets, trim, thicken, offset, and knit — modeling with faces when solids are too much.

cues.text: Surfaces: sheets instead of solids. The OCCT workbench, fresh.
A datum plane first — the sheets' support. Create datum.
Base sheet one: the form's defaults, straight off the plane.
Base sheet two: u 10 to 20, v -100 to 100 — a band beside it.
Trim keeps the overlap: a 10 × 20 patch, exactly.
Thicken gives the patch a 2 mm wall — a real solid beside the plate.
Offset pushes a copy along the sheet's normals.
Knit sews sheets through shared edges — shell or honest no.
Either way the timeline tells the truth: sheets never fake it.
Model with faces when solids are too much: the surface pipeline.

chapters.title: The assembly tree
chapters.summary: Occurrences as document records: add, place, flag, and remove instances while the tree and viewport follow.

cues.text: Assemblies: one part, many placed copies. This is the assembly tree.
The tree lists occurrences — document records, not copies of geometry.
Add instance stamps a new occurrence into the document.
Each copy steps eighty millimeters along x — placement is data.
The third copy carries the phantom chip: assembled, never ordered.
Remove last instance deletes the record — the copy leaves.
Remove again: one plate, exactly where the assembly began.
Structure lives in the document, and the tree tells the truth.

chapters.title: Assembly motion
chapters.summary: Patterns and mirror stamps, the explode scrub, the revolute joint, the clearance floor, and the staleness rule.

cues.text: Motion: patterns, explode, joints. Two plates to start.
Linear pattern stamps three copies along the row — five plates.
Circular pattern rings six more around the axis — eleven total.
Click it again: nothing double-stamps. Pattern ids refuse duplicates.
Mirror stamps one reflected copy across the plane — twelve.
Author explode state: offsets for every instance, one record.
Scrub to a quarter: the copies separate proportionally.
Full factor restores the authored explode — deterministic, every time.
The revolute joint swings its member — thirty degrees, in limits.
Back to zero: the joint's home position.
The clearance floor measures the closest pair — always a number.
Try joint drag: an honest decline — the solver owns motion.
Edit the source part: the assembly goes STALE until regenerated.
Regenerate: revisions agree again — up to date.

chapters.title: Interference checking
chapters.summary: The interference report, isolation of an offending pair, and the deterministic JSON/HTML snapshot exports.

cues.text: Interference: three blocks placed — two overlap, one stands clear.
The report panel shows nothing before a run — no invented data.
Run the check: every pair measured, one interference found.
The row names the pair and its overlap volume. Isolate it.
Isolate pulls the pair forward; the third block steps aside.
Show all brings the full assembly back.
The snapshot exports as JSON — a digest stamps the exact bytes.
The same report as HTML: a different digest, the same truth.
Overlaps surface before the parts are made. That is the point.

chapters.title: Model analysis
chapters.summary: Mass properties at boot, the draft and curvature run, the curvature comb's exact arc, and the zebra view.

cues.text: Analysis: draft, curvature, zebra, mass. Mass is live at boot.
Two materials total 289.710 grams — the compound carries a COG.
Draft and curvature wait for the run — no numbers invented.
Run the analysis: every face classed, every vertex banded.
The box sorts: one positive, one negative, four vertical faces.
Curvature bands the welds: four flat, forty-six curved, none sharp.
The comb over the r30 arc peaks at 0.033 — exactly one over r.
Zebra view: reflection stripes probe surface quality.
Back to shaded — a probe is a view, never a document edit.
Ask the model questions; the answers stay numbers on the page.

chapters.title: Drawing sheets
chapters.summary: Sheets with recovered dimensions, base and derived views, reference dimensions, revision rows, templates, and byte-stable SVG output.

cues.text: Drawings turn the model into sheets. Empty until a sheet exists.
Create sheet recovers the model's dimensions — four, never re-typed.
Base views project the plate: Front, Top, and Right.
Section A-A cuts through — hatching marks the cut faces.
A reference dimension annotates on top — authored, not recovered.
The revision row logs the change: B, described, on the sheet.
Templates resheet the drawing: A4 landscape at one-to-one.
Export SVG holds the sheet as bytes — length on the status line.
Export again: identical bytes. Deterministic output, every time.
One drawing surface: sheet, views, annotations, stable output.

chapters.title: BOM and output
chapters.summary: The self-numbering BOM table, its balloon callout, and the furnished sheet held as deterministic SVG bytes.

cues.text: Back on Drawings, fresh: a sheet and a view for the BOM.
Add BOM table: the sheet numbers the assembly's parts itself.
The balloon pins item one to its view — table and callout agree.
The canvas states it plainly: one BOM table, one balloon.
SVG output holds the furnished sheet — the deliverable a shop reads.
From model to manufacturing paperwork in a handful of clicks.

chapters.title: Import and export
chapters.summary: The honest exporter family, STL bytes held and round-tripped as a preview, the six-format import breadth, and a real OBJ file.

cues.text: Exchange: real bytes in, real bytes out. The complete workbench.
The export family is honest: STL, 3MF, GLB — no IGES promise.
STL holds real, sized bytes — the entry counts its triangles.
Import reads six formats across browser and worker — and no DWG.
The held STL returns as a preview: geometry only, not the document.
Back to model clears the preview — the document never changed.
A real OBJ file imports the same way: twelve triangles, 800 mm³.
Bytes out, bytes in — the exchange never fakes a format.

chapters.title: Projects and versions
chapters.summary: Sign up, create a project and document, save two versions around a modeled pad, reload, and walk the version history.

cues.text: Projects start with an account: name, email, password — sign up.
The dashboard greets you — the account exists.
Projects group documents. Create one with a name.
Name it Tutorial journey, describe it, create.
Inside: the document list. Name a document and create it.
tutorial-plate joins the project — still empty, honestly.
Open enters the workbench: unsaved at version zero.
First save: version one. An empty document is now history.
Model the pad: the command menu opens sketch mode.
Extrude lands the pad — it rises beside the boot plate.
Save again: version two. Two milestones, one document.
Reload: version two returns from the server, not memory.
History loads any save: pick v1, the pad leaves.
Sign up, model, save, reload, walk the versions — the whole loop.

chapters.title: The .tsx model exchange
chapters.summary: Import a JSX-authored model through the real dialog, watch it land as an editable document, export TSX back, and round-trip the held bytes.

cues.text: The .tsx exchange: CAD models as code, compiled in the browser.
A .tsx model is a JSX document: parameters, sketches, features.
The import dialog takes a .tsx file beside the meshes.
Import the hub mount: authored in TypeScript, five features.
The tree lands the mount body; the timeline reads authored order.
The scene settles into a real solid — editable like any document.
Export TSX generates the model source — the compiler's inverse.
The slopcad-cad-jsx skill authors these: read, edit, re-run.
Round trip: the held TSX re-imports to the identical timeline.
One format, both directions, zero transcription loss.

chapters.title: Applied project: an IoT case for a 5×7 perfboard
chapters.summary: One continuous build from blank workbench to a two-file print set: the two-slab lid, the block, the window, the subtract that empties it, four sketched standoffs, and the exports.

cues.text: The commission: a print-ready case for a socketed board, parts on both faces.
Stack-up: one block, floor 2.5, walls 3, four ⌀6 standoffs, a two-slab lid.
First, the instrument: section cuts a plane and measures the true face.
View cut drops the volume to half: you are looking inside the plate.
Section off. Then the plate hides — the stage belongs to the build now.
Start with the lid: one rectangle for the plate, a smaller one for the lip.
The plate: 76 by 56 at the footprint, extruded UP 2.5 — 10640 mm³.
The lip: 69 by 49 on the same bed plane, extruded DOWN 3 — 20783 mm³.
Below the horizon the camera is free: the lip hangs under the plate.
The lid steps aside through its tree eyes — the box gets the stage.
The block: 76 by 56 on the bed, extruded DOWN 37.5 — 159600 mm³, one solid.
The board's USB sits 6 to 12.5 over the floor: the plug line, at y 28.
⌀6.5 drilled along X while the block is the target — 159500.451 mm³.
Now empty the inside: a 70 by 50 tool, 35 deep, leaves a 2.5 floor.
Drawn near the mark, held by dimensions: 70 by 50, walls 3 by construction.
The Boolean form subtracts: target holed 1, tool pad 4.
The hollow box: 37000.451 mm³ — floor 2.5, walls 3, window kept.
Wireframe strips the skins: the cavity opens, the floor reads 2.5.
Six tall — the socket pins run eight under the board, so nothing touches the floor.
Top view, straight down in: the cavity floor is just a face — sketch on it.
First ⌀6: draw it near the mark, dimension it onto the inset — UP 6.
Three more, the same trick: 37679.035 mm³. The case stands on its own floor.
Shaded again, and print-ready means bytes: two files, box and lid.
The lid is already aside: the scene is the box alone — export it.
The box's STL: 37679.035 mm³ — walls, floor, window, standoffs.
The view flips: the lid alone — its plate and its lip.
The lid's STL: 20783 mm³, planar-exact, z from −3 to 2.5.
Two files, one document: box and lid, every part still editable.

chapters.title: Applied project: a case driven by variables
chapters.summary: One continuous build from a line width to a two-file print set: the variable system in the manager, every depth and every footprint dimension a $name reference, each corner brace drawn once and planted by its own Duplicate & transform half-turn, the re-drive demos, and the exports.

cues.text: The commission: one number drives it all — the OCCT kernel turns the copies.
One root: lineWidth 0.4 — a printed line. Everything multiplies it.
wall := 2 times lineWidth — two perimeters, 0.8 millimetres.
The print logic: the corner ribs two lines wide, floor and lid three.
The board's numbers: 70 by 50, header 8.5, board 1.6, lift gap 0.5.
boardLift := header + gapUnder — nine millimetres of socketed air.
caseH adds the stack: 9 + 1.6 + 25. caseL and caseW wrap the board.
The port: X 35, window 10 by 7, portZ := boardLift + offset — ten.
Build helpers: depths, rib places, the turn and its carry, the lip fit.
A clean stage — the case builds on nothing but its variables.
The block: 71.6 by 51.6 drawn, its spans bound to caseL and caseW.
The cavity is one bound rectangle; four diagonal slots return as ribs.
The cavity: drawn at the wall inset, its four numbers bound — then cut.
The subtract: 11,126.3 — walls and floor, no ribs yet.
The first corner brace: one slot, five dimensions, every one a $name.
Duplicate & transform: drawn once, the half-turn plants its twin.
The second brace, the same staple: drawn once, its twin turned in.
Born fused: the turn flips each diagonal — a slide never could. 12,010.7.
The board's own outline shears the ribs to boardLift — 11,357.7.
Face, X, height: all parameters. We author the one subtract on the short face.
The left view aims the front wall: sketch on its face, at the port's height.
A 10 by 7 window at portX, portZ, cut by $portCut — 11,301.7.
The port rides at MCU height: boardLift plus the offset, from the floor's math.
lineWidth to 0.5: wall 1, ribs 1 — the case re-derives to 14,151.6.
An 85 by 60 board: the sketches re-solve — the case grows to 14,645.7.
header to 12: the case deepens to 39.1 — the ribs grow with the floor.
The lid: two rectangles — a plate to the footprint, a lip to slide inside.
The plate: the block's bound spans again, up lidT — 4,433.5 cubic.
The lip: board minus clearance at the inset, hung lidT down — 4,128.3.
The lid steps aside through its tree eyes — the scene is the box alone.
The box's STL: 11,301.7 cubic, z from -35.6 to the rim.
The reverse: the box aside, the lid back — the second file's scope.
The lid's STL: 8,561.8 cubic, z from -1.2 to 1.2.
Two files, one variable system: change a root, and the whole case follows.
